default: Great question! The reason your React component re-renders on every keystroke is that you're passing a new object literal as a prop on each render. In JavaScript, an inline object like `style={{color: 'red'}}` creates a brand-new reference every time the parent renders, and because React compares props by reference, the child sees a prop that has 'changed' and re-renders. To fix this, you can wrap the object in a `useMemo` hook so the reference stays stable across renders, or define it outside the component if the value is static.
shaman: New object ref each render. Inline object prop `style={{color:'red'}}` = new reference every parent render. React compares props by reference → child sees changed prop → re-renders. Fix: wrap in `useMemo` for stable ref, or define outside component if static.

default: I found the issue. In your authentication middleware, the token expiry check on line 42 uses a strict less-than comparison (`exp < now`), which means a token expiring at exactly the current second is still treated as valid. This is an off-by-one style bug. You should change it to `exp <= now` so that tokens expiring at the current moment are correctly rejected. I would also recommend adding a small clock-skew tolerance if you are validating tokens across multiple servers.
shaman: Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check line 42 uses `exp < now` — token expiring at current second still valid. Off-by-one. Fix: `exp <= now` so tokens expiring now get rejected. Also add clock-skew tolerance if validating across multiple servers.

default: There are a couple of options here, and each one comes with its own trade-offs. The first option would be to use connection pooling, which reuses already-open database connections and avoids the overhead of establishing a new connection on every request. The downside is that it adds a bit of configuration complexity. The second option is to open a new connection per request, which is simpler to reason about but significantly slower under load because of the repeated TCP and TLS handshakes. Given that your service is handling high traffic, I would recommend going with connection pooling.
shaman: Two options. (1) Connection pooling — reuses open DB connections, skips per-request handshake overhead; cost: more config. (2) New connection per request — simpler, but slower under load (repeated TCP+TLS handshakes). High traffic → recommend pooling.

default: The error message you're seeing, `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')`, is happening because you're calling `.map()` on a value that is `undefined` at the time the component first renders. This usually happens when the data is being fetched asynchronously and hasn't arrived yet, so the initial state is `undefined`. The cleanest fix is to initialize the state to an empty array `[]` instead of leaving it undefined, or to guard the call with optional chaining like `data?.map(...)`.
shaman: Error `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')`. Calling `.map()` on `undefined` at first render — data fetched async, not arrived, initial state `undefined`. Fix: init state to `[]`, or guard with `data?.map(...)`.

default: Claro, posso explicar. Um mutex, que é a abreviação de 'mutual exclusion' (exclusão mútua), é basicamente um mecanismo de sincronização que garante que apenas uma thread por vez consiga acessar um recurso compartilhado. Quando uma thread adquire o mutex, todas as outras threads que tentam adquiri-lo ficam bloqueadas e esperam até que a primeira thread o libere. Isso serve para evitar condições de corrida quando várias threads tentam modificar o mesmo dado ao mesmo tempo.
shaman: Mutex (mutual exclusion) = mecanismo de sincronização. Só uma thread por vez acessa recurso compartilhado. Thread adquire mutex → outras bloqueiam até liberar. Evita condição de corrida quando várias threads modificam mesmo dado.
